title: Best Sleep Supplements of 2026
intro_mdx_or_text: Sleep supplements are a loosely regulated market where marketing routinely outruns the evidence, and effects are almost always smaller than sleep-hygiene fundamentals or treating an underlying disorder. For this 2026 ranking we scored five widely searched products against a five-criterion methodology, weighting Safety 30% and Evidence 30% most heavily, then Cost & Value 20%, Transparency 10%, and Support 10%. We prioritized single-ingredient formulas with published human trials, real per-serving doses, and independent quality testing over proprietary blends and sub-therapeutic gummies. We deliberately include non-affiliate options so our picks aren't limited to products that pay us. None of these replace a clinician's evaluation of persistent insomnia, and several interact with sedatives, antidepressants, and blood-pressure medications. Talk to a clinician before starting any sleep supplement, especially if you are pregnant, on prescription drugs, or dealing with chronic sleep problems that last more than a few weeks.
answer_block: Our top-rated sleep supplement for 2026 is Nature Made Melatonin 3 mg, scoring 8.2/10 in our five-criterion evaluation, and it is a product Firsthand earns no commission on. Melatonin has the largest human evidence base here: a 19-trial meta-analysis of 1,683 people found it shortens time to fall asleep and modestly improves sleep quality, and Nature Made carries USP verification that independently checks label accuracy at roughly $0.08 a day. It works best for circadian problems like jet lag and shift work, not routine insomnia. Doctor's Best High Absorption Magnesium (8.0) is our best evidence-backed alternative, with trials showing about 17 minutes faster sleep onset in older adults. Combination gummies like OLLY Sleep (6.6) rank lowest because a 2023 JAMA analysis found 22 of 25 melatonin gummies were inaccurately labeled. Our rankings weight Safety and Evidence at 30% each; commissions never influence placement. Persistent insomnia deserves a clinician, not escalating doses.

faq.question: What is the best sleep supplement in 2026?
faq.answer: No supplement works for everyone. Nature Made Melatonin 3 mg scored highest in our evaluation because melatonin has the largest human evidence base and Nature Made is USP verified and inexpensive, but it helps most with circadian issues like jet lag rather than chronic insomnia. Magnesium glycinate is the best-studied alternative for general sleep quality. Effects for all of them are modest compared with treating an underlying sleep disorder.

faq.question: Is it safe to take sleep supplements every night?
faq.answer: Short-term use of melatonin, magnesium (within the 350 mg/day supplemental limit), glycine, and L-theanine is generally well tolerated in healthy adults. Long-term nightly use is less studied, and these can interact with sedatives, antidepressants, and blood-pressure medications. Melatonin's long-term safety data is limited. Talk to a clinician before nightly use, especially if you are pregnant or on prescription drugs.

faq.question: Does melatonin help with insomnia or just jet lag?
faq.answer: Melatonin most reliably shifts sleep timing for jet lag, shift work, and delayed sleep phase. For chronic insomnia, NCCIH says there is not enough strong evidence to recommend it, and clinical guidelines do not consider it a first-line insomnia treatment. Persistent insomnia deserves a clinician's evaluation rather than escalating melatonin doses.

faq.question: Do you earn money from these recommendations?
faq.answer: Some links on this page are affiliate links, and we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We also deliberately include non-affiliate options — our top pick, Nature Made Melatonin, and NOW Glycine both earn us nothing. Commissions never influence our rankings, scores, or ordering; a product that pays us can and does rank below one that doesn't.

title: Best Weight-Loss Supplements of 2026
intro_mdx_or_text: Weight-loss supplements are a crowded, heavily marketed category where confident promises rarely match the published evidence. Most branded fat burners have never been tested as finished products in a controlled trial; instead they lean on individual ingredients whose effects, where measurable at all, tend to be small and only meaningful alongside a reduced-calorie diet and exercise. We approached this list as skeptics. Rather than reward slick copy, our scoring weights Safety at 30%, Evidence at 30%, Cost and Value at 20%, Transparency at 10%, and Support at 10%. Products with proprietary blends that hide doses, thin clinical support, or aggressive auto-ship and refund terms are marked down hard. The one option here with genuinely strong randomized-trial data is not a supplement at all but an FDA-approved over-the-counter drug. Read the cons as carefully as the pros.
answer_block: Our top pick is Alli (orlistat 60 mg), the only FDA-approved over-the-counter weight-loss aid, which scores 7.5/10. It is the sole product here backed by large randomized trials: in a pooled analysis of 16 orlistat trials (over 10,000 participants), it produced roughly 2.9 kg more weight loss than placebo over a year, alongside well-documented gastrointestinal side effects. Be honest about the category, though. Most branded fat burners rely on ingredients with weak or null evidence; one systematic review of 315 randomized trials found only 16 showed a significant weight difference versus control. Among the direct-response supplements we reviewed, Transparent Labs Fat Burner (6.5) rates highest mainly for disclosing every dose, while proprietary-blend products like Java Burn (4.4) and Ikaria Lean Belly Juice (4.0) score lowest. No pill replaces diet and exercise, and any supplement here should be treated as optional, not essential.

faq.question: Do you earn money from these recommendations?
faq.answer: Yes, for some of them. Several products on this list are monetized, meaning we may earn a commission if you buy through our links; those are labeled. Our top pick, Alli (orlistat), is not monetized. Affiliate relationships never change a product's score, which is driven by our published rubric weighting safety and evidence most heavily.

faq.question: Do weight loss supplements actually work?
faq.answer: Mostly not to a degree you would notice. A systematic review of 315 randomized trials of purported weight-loss supplements found only 16 demonstrated a statistically significant weight difference versus control, and the differences ranged from about 0.3 to 4.93 kg. The one strongly evidence-backed option here is orlistat, an FDA-approved drug, not a supplement. Any product may support weight management only alongside a reduced-calorie diet and exercise.

faq.question: What is the safest weight loss supplement?
faq.answer: No supplement is risk-free, and products with undisclosed proprietary blends make safety hard to judge. Among options here, the FDA-approved OTC drug orlistat has the best-characterized safety profile, though it causes gastrointestinal side effects and carries rare warnings about liver and kidney injury. Caffeine-heavy fat burners can cause jitteriness, insomnia, and raised heart rate. Talk to a clinician before starting any product.

faq.question: Are weight loss supplements FDA approved?
faq.answer: Dietary supplements are not FDA-approved before sale; the FDA does not evaluate them for effectiveness before they reach the market. Only Alli (orlistat 60 mg) on this list is an actual FDA-approved over-the-counter drug. The branded fat burners here are marketed as dietary supplements and legally cannot claim to treat or cure any disease.

title: Top GLP-1 Weight-Loss Telehealth Providers of 2026
intro_mdx_or_text: GLP-1 telehealth pricing was rewritten in 2025-2026. The FDA declared the semaglutide shortage resolved in February 2025, the legal basis for mass-compounded copies wound down, and Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly began selling Wegovy and Zepbound direct-to-consumer, pricing that most telehealth platforms now simply pass through. This directory compares six providers that verifiably operate in July 2026, from branded-only platforms (Ro, WeightWatchers Clinic, Sesame, Hims & Hers) to programs still centered on compounded medication (Mochi Health, Noom Med). Each entry separates the membership fee from the medication cost, spells out what the fee actually buys (labs, synchronous visits, insurance coordination), and lists provider-specific red flags. Scores weight Safety 30%, Evidence 30%, Cost & Value 20%, Transparency 10%, and Support 10%. All GLP-1 medications are prescription-only and require a provider evaluation; nothing here promises a treatment outcome.
answer_block: Ro Body scores highest in our 2026 comparison at 8.4/10. Ro prescribes only FDA-approved GLP-1s and passes through manufacturer direct-pay pricing, with the Wegovy pen from $199/month and the Zepbound KwikPen at $299-$449/month, on top of a membership that costs $39 the first month and then $149/month (as low as $74/month prepaid annually), with an insurance concierge for covered patients. WeightWatchers Clinic (8.3/10) is the strongest pick when insurance coordination matters most, and Sesame (8.2/10) is the value pick, with labs included from $59-$99/month. Efficacy belongs to the medications, not the platforms: in the randomized STEP 1 trial, semaglutide 2.4 mg produced a 14.9% mean body-weight reduction over 68 weeks versus 2.4% with placebo. Every option requires an eligibility screen and a licensed clinician's prescription; approval is never guaranteed.

faq.question: Is compounded semaglutide still legal and safe in 2026?
faq.answer: Mass compounding was allowed only while FDA listed semaglutide and tirzepatide in shortage; those shortages were declared resolved in 2025, so pharmacies may now compound copies only for patients whose medical needs cannot be met by the approved product. Compounded GLP-1s are not FDA-reviewed for safety, effectiveness, or quality, and published case reports document 10-fold dosing errors from compounded vials. Providers still centered on compounded medication carry regulatory and supply risk.

faq.question: Will insurance cover GLP-1 weight-loss medication through telehealth?
faq.answer: Sometimes. Coverage for Wegovy and Zepbound varies widely by plan and often requires prior authorization. WeightWatchers Clinic and Ro assign insurance coordinators to pursue coverage; Sesame accepts insurance for medications (copays can be as low as $25/month). Membership or program fees themselves are almost always self-pay.

faq.question: What does GLP-1 telehealth actually cost per month in 2026?
faq.answer: Two bills: a program fee ($0-$149/month, e.g., $74/month at WeightWatchers Clinic or $59-$99/month at Sesame with labs included) plus medication (cash-pay branded GLP-1s run $149-$499/month at manufacturer direct rates; compounded programs run $99-$299/month all-in). Typical all-in cash-pay totals are roughly $250-$600/month.

faq.question: Can I get a GLP-1 prescription without seeing a doctor?
faq.answer: No. Every legitimate platform requires evaluation by a licensed clinician, and BMI-based eligibility criteria apply (generally BMI >= 30, or >= 27 with a weight-related condition). Some platforms use asynchronous questionnaires rather than video visits, which is faster but means less clinical screening, and platforms with no lab work or live visit deserve extra scrutiny.

title: Best Teeth Whitening & Oral Health Products of 2026
intro_mdx_or_text: Teeth whitening is a cosmetic bleaching problem with a well-understood chemistry: hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide oxidizes stain molecules, and concentration plus contact time drive results. Marketing, however, has outrun the evidence, so we graded every product against the peer-reviewed record rather than brand claims. Our score weights Safety 30% (peroxide concentration, sensitivity and gingival-irritation risk), Evidence 30% (published clinical data for the actual product or its active), Cost & Value 20% (price per treatment and subscription traps), Transparency 10% (clear ingredient and claim disclosure), and Support 10% (returns, guarantees, service). We prioritize products with real trial data and honest labeling, which is why a non-monetized drugstore staple can outrank pricier direct-to-consumer kits. LED gadgets and oral probiotics are held to the same bar. Prices were verified on brand and retailer sites on 2026-07-11.
answer_block: Our top pick is Crest 3D Whitestrips Professional Effects (8.5/10), the most heavily studied at-home whitener you can buy without a subscription. Peroxide strips have the strongest clinical record of any OTC format: in one randomized trial, 10% hydrogen peroxide strips produced significant whitening within a single week, and the ADA grants its Seal of Acceptance to whitening strips that meet safety and efficacy standards. Expect mild, temporary tooth sensitivity, reported in 15-78% of people across bleaching studies, which resolves after treatment stops. At roughly $45-$51 for 22 treatments (about $2 per session) with no auto-ship, it beats LED kits and boutique strips on both evidence and value. Skip products that lean on hardware or bacteria over peroxide: light activation adds little to strong gels, and a major systematic review found current evidence insufficient to recommend oral probiotics for managing dental disease. Whiten with peroxide, protect your gums, and see a dentist first.

faq.question: Do you earn money from these recommendations?
faq.answer: Some links are affiliate links, meaning we may earn a commission if you buy through them at no extra cost to you. Our top pick, Crest 3D Whitestrips Professional Effects, is not monetized, and monetized products never rank higher because they pay us. Scores come only from published evidence, safety data, price and transparency.

faq.question: What is the best over-the-counter teeth whitening product?
faq.answer: For most people, hydrogen-peroxide whitening strips are the best-evidenced OTC option. They deliver measurable color change in clinical trials and are inexpensive per treatment. Whitening toothpaste helps with surface stains but changes tooth color far less than a peroxide strip or gel.

faq.question: Do led teeth whitening lights actually work?
faq.answer: The light itself does little. A systematic review and meta-analysis of in-office bleaching found no meaningful efficacy benefit from light activation with high-concentration peroxide, while light raised the odds of tooth sensitivity roughly 3.5-fold. The peroxide gel does the whitening; the LED is largely for show.

faq.question: Does teeth whitening damage enamel?
faq.answer: Used as directed, peroxide whiteners have not been shown to permanently damage enamel, but they commonly cause temporary tooth sensitivity and can irritate gums on contact. The ADA advises talking to a dentist before whitening, especially if you have restorations, gum recession or untreated decay.

title: Best Fitness Apps of 2026
intro_mdx_or_text: Fitness apps make it easier to start exercising at home, but no app does the work for you. Research on smartphone activity apps shows small average gains, strongest in the first few months, so the best app is the one you keep using. The benchmark we score against is the federal Physical Activity Guidelines: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening work for all major muscle groups on 2 or more days. For this 2026 ranking we compared four apps with official, published pricing, from a free option to a full-access subscription, using our five criteria: Safety 30%, Evidence 30%, Cost & Value 20%, Transparency 10% and Support 10%. None of these apps has a published clinical trial of its own, so evidence scores are equal and reflect exercise research in general. Firsthand does not do hands-on testing; this ranking is based on official documentation and published research. Check with a clinician before starting a new exercise program if you have a heart condition, are pregnant or have other health concerns.
answer_block: Our top fitness app for 2026 is Nike Training Club, scoring 7.2/10, mainly because it is free and still covers strength, HIIT and yoga with structured programs. Apple Fitness+ (7.1) is the best paid value for iPhone users at $9.99 a month or $79.99 a year, shareable with up to five family members (as of 2026-10-02). Fitbod (6.9) is the pick for adaptive strength training at $95.99 a year. The Peloton App (6.7) suits people who own a bike, treadmill or rower, but App+ costs $28.99 a month and Peloton's own page quotes two different prices. Keep expectations realistic: a meta-analysis of randomized trials found activity apps raised daily steps by a small, non-significant amount on average, with the best results in the first three months. Aim for the federal target of 150 minutes of moderate activity plus strength work twice a week. Firsthand earns no commission on any app here.

faq.question: What is the best fitness app in 2026?
faq.answer: Nike Training Club scored highest in our review because it is free and covers strength, HIIT and yoga. If you have an iPhone and want more polish, Apple Fitness+ is good value. For strength training that adapts to your equipment, Fitbod is the strongest choice.

faq.question: Do fitness apps actually work?
faq.answer: They can help, but effects are modest. A 2019 meta-analysis of randomized trials found a small, non-significant average rise in daily steps, with apps working best over the first three months. The health benefit comes from the exercise itself.

faq.question: How much exercise do I need each week?
faq.answer: The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans recommend 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous aerobic activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days.

faq.question: Do you earn money from these recommendations?
faq.answer: No. Firsthand earns no commission on any app in this ranking. Scores come only from our published rubric.

title: Best OTC Hearing Aids of 2026
intro_mdx_or_text: Since FDA created the over-the-counter hearing aid category in 2022, adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss can buy a hearing aid without a prescription or exam. For this 2026 ranking we only considered devices with an FDA authorization we could look up in FDA's own databases, and that the maker still sells. Two well-known brands, Eargo and Lexie, were left out because their websites say their US parent is winding down operations. We scored four options against our published methodology, weighting Safety 30% and Evidence 30%, then Cost & Value 20%, Transparency 10% and Support 10%. Firsthand does not test devices by hand; scores come from regulatory records, published studies and the makers' own terms. The research on self-fitting aids is encouraging but young: a 2026 meta-analysis found outcomes comparable to professional fitting with low certainty, and a 2025 trial found full audiologist care still scored higher. FDA advises seeing a clinician first if you have sudden or one-sided hearing loss, ear pain, drainage or dizziness.
answer_block: Our top-rated OTC hearing aid for 2026 is Apple AirPods Pro 3 with the Hearing Aid feature, scoring 7.8/10, and Firsthand earns nothing on it. FDA granted the feature De Novo authorization in 2024 after a 118-person study found self-fitting gave similar perceived benefit to professional fitting, and at $249 it is the cheapest FDA-authorized option here, though it needs an iPhone or iPad and has a 14-day return window. Jabra Enhance Select (7.7) is the pick for support, with a 100-day trial and 3 years of remote audiology, at $1,195 to $1,995. Concha Sol (7.3) suits people who prefer disposable batteries, and Sennheiser All-Day Clear (7.1) is the lowest-cost dedicated aid at $999.95 but carries only a 1-year warranty. All four are for adults with perceived mild to moderate loss. Sudden or one-sided hearing changes need a clinician.

faq.question: Who should buy an OTC hearing aid?
faq.answer: FDA says OTC hearing aids are for adults 18 and older with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss, the kind where you hear in quiet but struggle in groups or noise. They have limited maximum output and may not be enough for severe loss.

faq.question: Are self-fitting OTC hearing aids as good as ones fitted by an audiologist?
faq.answer: Close, on average, but not identical. A 2026 meta-analysis of 15 studies found comparable outcomes with low certainty of evidence, while a 2025 randomized trial of 245 adults found audiologist-fitted care scored modestly higher than OTC models.

faq.question: When should I see a doctor instead?
faq.answer: FDA lists sudden hearing change within the past 6 months, hearing loss worse in one ear, ear drainage, pain or dizziness, and ringing in only one ear as reasons to see a healthcare professional before buying an OTC hearing aid.

faq.question: Why are Eargo and Lexie not in this ranking?
faq.answer: Both brands' websites carry a notice that their US parent entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in July 2026 and is winding down, with app support and customer service ending in October 2026. We only rank products that are still sold and supported.

title: Best Home Blood Pressure Monitors of 2026
intro_mdx_or_text: A home blood pressure monitor is only useful if its readings are accurate, and many are not. A 2020 study of one national online market found only 18.3% of upper-arm cuff monitors on sale had been validated. For this 2026 ranking we only considered monitors listed on the US Blood Pressure Validated Device Listing (validatebp.org), the AMA-backed list where an independent committee decides whether a device meets accuracy criteria, and that the maker currently sells. We scored four upper-arm monitors against our published methodology, weighting Safety 30% and Evidence 30%, then Cost & Value 20%, Transparency 10% and Support 10%. Firsthand does not test devices by hand; scores come from the validation listing, published research and the makers' own specifications and terms. The AHA and AMA say home monitoring is a validated way to measure blood pressure outside the clinic, and a 52-study review found it lowers blood pressure compared with usual care. A monitor supports care from a clinician; it does not replace it. Check that your arm fits the listed cuff range, and share your readings.
answer_block: Our top-rated home blood pressure monitor for 2026 is the OMRON Platinum BP5465, scoring 8.6/10, and Firsthand earns nothing on it. It is on the US Blood Pressure Validated Device Listing, averages three readings automatically, stores readings for two users and carries a six-year warranty for a $90.99 MSRP. The OMRON 5 Series BP7255 (8.4) is a validated single-user option at $83.99 with a 130/80 indicator. Withings BPM Connect (7.9) is the VDL-listed pick for pregnancy and syncs over Wi-Fi, at $129.95. Withings BPM Vision (7.7) is validated to the newest standard here and listed with an XL cuff, but costs $179.95. Every monitor here passed independent validation, which matters more than any app feature. Share your readings with a clinician rather than acting on them alone.

faq.question: What does 'validated' mean for a blood pressure monitor?
faq.answer: It means the device's accuracy was tested against a recognized protocol, such as ANSI/AAMI/ISO 81060-2, and reviewed. The US Blood Pressure Validated Device Listing at validatebp.org publishes devices that an independent review committee found meet its criteria. Check your exact model number, since similar-looking models can differ.

faq.question: Are upper-arm monitors better than wrist monitors?
faq.answer: The AHA and AMA statement says validated oscillometric devices are preferred for home monitoring. All four picks here are validated upper-arm models, and the validation list also includes some wrist devices.

faq.question: How should I take readings at home?
faq.answer: The AHA and AMA recommend following a standardized protocol with a validated device. Monitors like the OMRON Platinum can average three readings for you. Bring your log or app data to your clinician.

faq.question: Can a home monitor diagnose high blood pressure?
faq.answer: No. Home readings help a clinician confirm a diagnosis, spot white-coat or masked hypertension and track treatment, but the diagnosis and treatment decisions belong to your clinician.

title: Best Mental Health Apps and Online Therapy of 2026
intro_mdx_or_text: This ranking covers two different kinds of help. Online therapy services such as Talkspace and BetterHelp connect you with a licensed therapist for treatment. Self-guided apps such as Headspace and Calm teach meditation and stress skills, which can ease everyday stress but do not replace treatment. We scored all four against our five criteria: Safety 30%, Evidence 30%, Cost & Value 20%, Transparency 10% and Support 10%. Safety includes how each company has handled your data, since mental health information is highly sensitive. Evidence favors randomized trials of the product itself, and we note when study authors worked for the company. Firsthand does not test services by hand; this review is based on official pricing and policy pages, regulator actions and published research. None of these services is for emergencies. If you are in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, which is free, confidential and open 24/7, or call 911.
answer_block: Our top pick for 2026 is Headspace at 7.8/10, a self-guided meditation app with published randomized trials and a price of $69.99 a year in the US App Store (as of 2026-10-02). If you need treatment from a licensed therapist, Talkspace (7.5) is our top therapy platform: therapists are licensed in your state, it works with major insurers including Medicare plans, and a randomized trial found its message-based therapy was noninferior to video therapy for depression. Calm (7.4) is a close alternative to Headspace with wider device support. BetterHelp (6.4) ranks last because of its 2023 FTC order to pay $7.8 million over sharing users' health data for advertising, and because its price varies by referral source. Apps help most with everyday stress; a 2024 meta-analysis found small effects on depression and anxiety symptoms. Not for emergencies: call or text 988 in the US. Firsthand earns no commission on any service here.

faq.question: What is the best mental health app in 2026?
faq.answer: Headspace scored highest in our review for low cost and published trials. For therapy with a licensed professional, Talkspace scored highest among the platforms we reviewed because of insurance coverage, psychiatry access and randomized trial data.

faq.question: Is online therapy as good as in-person therapy?
faq.answer: For some conditions, the research is encouraging. A meta-analysis of 20 trials found guided internet-delivered CBT produced effects equivalent to face-to-face CBT, though few conditions have been studied individually. Severe or complex conditions may still need in-person care.

faq.question: Can a meditation app replace therapy?
faq.answer: No. A 2024 meta-analysis of 45 trials found mindfulness apps give small reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms, and they did not beat active therapies. If symptoms persist or affect daily life, see a licensed clinician.

faq.question: What should I do in a mental health emergency?
faq.answer: Do not rely on an app or online therapy service. In the US, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, which is free, confidential and available 24/7, or call 911 if you are in immediate danger.

faq.answer: No. Firsthand earns no commission on any service in this ranking. Scores come only from our published rubric.

title: Best Vitamin D Supplements of 2026
intro_mdx_or_text: Vitamin D is one of the most popular supplements in the US, and the evidence is clearer than the marketing suggests. It is needed for calcium absorption and bone health, and many people fall short because few foods contain it. But large randomized trials in healthy adults who were not deficient, such as VITAL with over 25,000 participants, found that 2,000 IU a day did not reduce cancer, heart events or fractures. For this 2026 ranking we limited the field to single-ingredient vitamin D3 products whose third-party certification we could confirm on the certifier's own database, in this case NSF Certified for Sport. We then scored each against our five criteria: Safety 30%, Evidence 30%, Cost & Value 20%, Transparency 10% and Support 10%. Because every product shares the same ingredient, evidence scores are equal, and the ranking turns on dose, price and buying terms. Firsthand does not test products by hand; this is a documentation and evidence review. Ask a clinician about testing your level before taking vitamin D long term.
answer_block: Our top vitamin D supplement for 2026 is dotFIT Vitamin D-3 1,000 IU, scoring 8.0/10. It is NSF Certified for Sport, gives 1,000 IU per softgel (close to the adult RDA of 600 to 800 IU and well under the 4,000 IU upper limit listed by MedlinePlus), and costs $8.95 for 100 softgels, about 9 cents a day (as of 2026-10-02). Klean Athlete Klean-D 1000 (7.7) is the vegetarian tablet alternative, and Momentous Vitamin D3 2000 IU (7.6) is the pick for vegans. Thorne Vitamin D-5,000 (7.0) is well made, but its 5,000 IU dose is above the adult upper limit, so it suits clinician-guided use. Set expectations: in the VITAL trial, 2,000 IU of D3 a day did not lower fractures, cancer or heart events in healthy adults who were not deficient. Vitamin D corrects a shortfall; it is not a general health booster. Firsthand earns no commission on any product here.

faq.question: What is the best vitamin D supplement in 2026?
faq.answer: dotFIT Vitamin D-3 1,000 IU scored highest in our review because it is NSF Certified for Sport, uses a conservative dose, and costs about 9 cents a day. Any certified D3 at 1,000 to 2,000 IU will raise blood levels similarly; price and dietary needs (vegetarian or vegan) are the main differences.

faq.question: How much vitamin D should I take a day?
faq.answer: MedlinePlus lists an RDA of 600 IU a day for adults 19 to 70 and 800 IU for adults over 70, with a safe upper limit of 4,000 IU a day. Your clinician may recommend more if a blood test shows a deficiency. Count fortified foods and multivitamins toward your total.

faq.question: Does vitamin D prevent fractures or cancer?
faq.answer: Not in healthy adults who are not deficient, according to the best trial data. In VITAL, 2,000 IU of vitamin D3 a day did not lower invasive cancer, major cardiovascular events or fractures compared with placebo over about five years.

faq.question: Is D3 better than D2?
faq.answer: A 2012 meta-analysis of randomized trials found D3 raised blood vitamin D levels more than D2 overall, mostly with large bolus doses; with daily dosing the difference was not significant. All four products here use D3.

faq.question: Do you earn money from these recommendations?
faq.answer: No. Firsthand earns no commission on any product in this ranking. Scores come only from our published rubric.

title: Best Prenatal Vitamins of 2026
intro_mdx_or_text: An independent check on what is in the bottle is the first thing we look for in a supplement. For this 2026 ranking of prenatal vitamins we only considered products that appear in NSF's NSF/ANSI 173 dietary supplement listings and that the maker currently sells. Several USP Verified Nature Made prenatals were left out because Nature Made's own pages mark them as no longer available. We scored four products against our published methodology, weighting Safety 30% and Evidence 30%, then Cost & Value 20%, Transparency 10% and Support 10%. Firsthand does not test supplements by hand; scores come from certification listings, NIH's label database, public health guidance and the makers' own pages. We checked each formula against the nutrients guidance names: folic acid (USPSTF, 400 to 800 mcg), iron (27 mg RDA in pregnancy), iodine (150 mcg advised by the American Thyroid Association), choline (450 mg intake level, rarely met by prenatals) and DHA. No prenatal replaces prenatal care. Agree your supplement plan, especially iron, with your clinician.
answer_block: Our top-rated prenatal vitamin for 2026 is TheraNatal Complete, scoring 7.7/10, and Firsthand earns nothing on it. It is NSF listed and covers iron at the 27 mg pregnancy RDA, iodine, 300 mg DHA and 250 mg choline, at about $0.97 a day across three pills. Thorne Basic Prenatal (7.2) is a transparent NSF-listed option with iodine and choline, but its 45 mg of iron equals the adult upper limit and it has no DHA. USPSTF recommends 400 to 800 mcg of folic acid daily for anyone who could become pregnant. Check iron and folate form with your clinician before choosing.

faq.question: What should a prenatal vitamin contain?
faq.answer: Guidance points to folic acid (USPSTF recommends 400 to 800 mcg daily for anyone who could become pregnant), iron (the pregnancy RDA is 27 mg), and iodine (the American Thyroid Association advises 150 mcg a day). Choline and DHA are often missing or low, so check the label.

faq.question: Are prenatal gummies as good as pills?
faq.answer: Gummies are easier to take, but the two gummies in this ranking contain little or no iron. If you choose a gummy, ask your clinician whether you need iron separately.

faq.question: What does NSF certification mean for a supplement?
faq.answer: Products listed under NSF/ANSI 173 have been certified by NSF against that dietary supplement standard. NSF advises confirming any listing directly on its own site.

faq.question: Can I take more than one prenatal or extra iron?
faq.answer: Do not stack supplements without advice. The adult upper limit for iron is 45 mg a day, and iron overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in young children, so keep bottles out of reach.
